No objection to theorizing.

The thing about the Spectre attacks is that they are attacks on these features in the abstract, rather than specific implementations. It's not some error in implementation, some fine point that they got wrong. Given speculation that's aggressive enough to do memory reads, it's going to affect the cache. At the core all of these attacks are getting things to speculatively execute, then finding the side-effects on the cache. Intel's is worst because they don't do a privilege check before the speculative loads; at least AMD stops this. The others don't involve privilege levels, so there's nothing to catch, just a clever exploitation of state leakage.

In general when you have a caching system, it sometimes gets wasted a little by loads that don't turn out to get used, but caching is a statistical game so as long as it increases overall performance it's good. But security is a details-matter thing, and every little trace something leaves behind can become a covert channel for some other piece of code to receive sensitive data.

2011? The problem has been around since the 1990s, when speculative execution went mainstream.

Obviously there is no conspiracy because AMD did great work avoiding the problem and almost succeeded.

Meltdown and Spectre are only the latest fiascos resulting from timing side channels. This type of problem has historically been quite difficult for people to understand and avoid. There are many devious ways to use timing information to breach secrecy.
